name: Printing Consecutive Numbers Starting from Zero (Case 1)
description: Construct a program that prints a sequence of numbers from 0 (inclusive) to 10 (exclusive).
code:
#Step 1: Iterate through the numbers in the sequence
for num in range(10): 
    #Step 1.1: Print each number in the sequence
    print(num)

commentList: This line starts a loop that goes through the numbers you want to print: it runs the indented block once for each number from 0 up to 9.

Breakdown: 'for' begins the loop, 'num' is the loop variable that holds each value in turn, 'in' connects the variable to the sequence, 'range(10)' produces the sequence, and the ':' marks the start of the indented loop body — you must indent the following lines.
Semantics: range(10) produces numbers starting at 0 (inclusive) and stopping before 10 (exclusive), so the loop will give you 0,1,2,...,9 in order.

Common errors & misconceptions: forgetting the ':' or wrong indentation causes a SyntaxError/IndentationError; expecting range(10) to include 10 is a common mistake (use range(11) if you need 0..10); passing a non-integer to range or using a float like range(10.0) will raise a TypeError.

Best practices: choose a clear loop variable name (num is fine here), avoid changing the loop variable inside the loop, and if you need an inclusive upper bound add 1 to the argument (e.g., range(0, end+1)).

Efficiency note: in Python 3, range(10) produces a lightweight iterable rather than a full list, so it's memory-efficient for large ranges — you don't need list(range(10)) unless you specifically need a list.

commentList: You use this line to display the current loop value so each number appears in the program output.
You are calling the print function with num as its argument: print(...) is the way to send text to the console in Python 3, and num is the loop variable defined by the for statement.
You must keep this line indented under the for loop so it runs once per iteration; if you unindent it, it will run only after the loop finishes.

Common mistakes to avoid: writing print num (missing parentheses) causes a syntax error in Python 3, misspelling num causes a NameError, or placing the line outside the loop will stop you from printing each number.
Remember that print adds a newline by default, so each call prints on its own line; if you want numbers on the same line use print(num, end=' ') or build a string with ' '.join for large outputs.

Best practice: keep printing simple while learning, but for large data avoid many print calls for performance reasons; when adding labels use f-strings like print(f"num: {num}") to make output clearer.

distractors.description: You might pick this because you think counting normally starts at 1, so you set the loop to begin at 1. Step-by-step: the loop will run with num taking values 1, 2, 3, ..., 9. That means 0 is never printed, so the output will be missing the first element the task asked for. There is no syntax error — the program runs — but the behavior is wrong because it omits 0. Compared to the intended behavior, this line changes only the starting value of the sequence, so the loop still iterates and prints numbers but begins one step too late. That is why this choice is a plausible but incorrect option.

You might choose this because you want the number 10 to appear and you believe the loop's end argument is included. Step-by-step: the loop will run with num = 0, 1, 2, ..., 10, so it prints an extra value (10) that the task wanted excluded. The program runs without error, but it prints one value too many. Using this line overshoots the requested sequence by including the endpoint; it alters the range's end rather than following the intended exclusive-end convention, so the output no longer matches the specification.

You might write this because you misunderstand the meaning of the third argument (step) and think 0 will either use a default or keep the same value. Step-by-step: when Python tries to create this range it will fail because a step of 0 is invalid. The program will raise an exception and crash instead of printing anything. This is different from a subtle output mistake — it causes a runtime error. The problem is the step argument is not a safe value here; replacing it with this distractor changes the loop's control semantics into an illegal state, so the program stops before producing the desired sequence.
